utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone after this long Easter weekend. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Harmon, is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness, which, as I understand, is Ramiz Alajbegovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We are, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, prior to that occurring, there are a number of matters that I would wish to deal with. Firstly, I have a number of objections to the statements that are proposed to be tendered under 89(f).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I e-mailed my objections to the Prosecution last night, and I also forwarded a copy to the Trial Chamber so that Your Honours would be aware of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have not received it this morning, but those who usually assist me in the early morning hours were late, I take it for technical reasons, so --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I can outline what those objections are now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Firstly, Your Honour, if you go -- do Your Honours have copies of the statement in front of you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I haven't got it for the same reason, not with me at the moment, but my colleagues have. So if there would be one additional copy. Yes. I've got them, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Just in relation to the first page of the statement, which is page 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I object to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that you are talking about the ICTY statement or --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour, yes, the statement dated January 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Page 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours. And that would be paragraphs -- yes, 6 to 10. Your Honours, the basis of the objection there is that it basically seems to talk about Serb nationalism and what have you in 1991. I object there on the basis that, Your Honour, in the context, I would submit it's irrelevant and also non-contextual. It just goes to Serb nationalism without referring to the context and the rise of nationalism amongst all parties at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is very relevant to what the Court will be considering. The Court has heard through a number of -- through the course of this trial testimony relating to the development of nationalism in various municipalities. This evidence is specifically relevant to the developments of what occurred in the Rogatica municipality, and I intend specifically to ask Mr. Alajbegovic about these two meetings and what the impact and significance of these two meetings were insofar as the political developments in the Rogatica municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Loukas, it's not entirely clear to me, do you say it's not relevant if it's not put next to other nationalist movements or --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Precisely, Your Honour. It's non-contextualism in essence makes it irrelevant because it becomes merely tendentious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But would you consider other nationalistic movements relevant? I mean, would this be something the --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we're going to mention Serb nationalism, then of course other nationalisms become relevant. But if we're only going to mention Serb nationalism in the context where -- in a country where three nationalist parties developed and there was nationalism developing among the three different groups, then in that sense it's non-contextual and it's only relevant if it's placed in context. If it's not placed in context, in my view, Your Honour, and in my submission, it's not relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Your observation suggests that there was other nationalist -- nationalism developing as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do not know. I mean, let's just assume for argument's sake that the Prosecution takes it that there was only one national movement. That could not even create the context you're asking for, whereas the Defence, if it takes the position that there was other nationalist -- there were other nationalistic developments as well, then of course it could create a context and --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I think it's also a problem with the way statements are taken. For example, the statements are often taken in quite a sloppy way, and prior to the introduction of 92 bis and prior to the introduction of the usage of 89(f) in this context, so they're actually taken in a context whereby it was always assumed that people would give their evidence viva voce in a proper form, not subject to leading questions, and objectionable material could be objected to when it was taken through in terms of proper evidence in chief. I have other objections to the statement that I can take you through, Your Honour, but this is the beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now I have heard. Unless there would be any further comment of Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your next objection would be, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Now, the next objection, we go to page 3, and that is the first full paragraph there after the list of names, that is paragraph 12, and we look at the last sentence there. Yes. "In my opinion, there was no threat to them whatsoever, and this was mainly an attempt to brainwash them and to encourage Serb nationalism." Now, Your Honour, I object to that on the basis of -- that it is opinion-based evidence, and it's not delineated there on what factual basis the opinion is based. So as an expression of mere opinion, I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, this is a witness who was the chief of the Uniform Police. He was a man who was a person significantly associated with the organs of the administration that existed in the Rogatica municipality at the time. I intend specifically to ask him about these people. I intend to specifically ask him about threats that he perceived during the course of the rise of the Serbian takeover of that municipality, and I do believe, Your Honour, that opinion would assist this Trial Chamber in judging the facts in this particular case. So therefore, I think an opinion, Your Honour, I will explore it with him, and I think it is a proper opinion to elicit given his knowledge of the facts and circumstances that existed in the Rogatica municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What you say as a matter of fact is that you're going to elicit the factual base for what is described here as an opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, whether there was any threat or not is not necessarily an opinion, but the second half of the line, of course, is an interpretation of why it was done. Mr. Harmon, would you have any problem in striking this from the statement and see what the witness could tell us in terms of the last part of paragraph 12?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have no objection to striking that, Your Honour. He's going to be describing the nationalistic context of these meetings before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it we'll hear his evidence on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, so therefore the Prosecution does not oppose taking out the line starting with, "In my opinion..." up to "Serb nationalism" at the end of paragraph 12. Your next objection, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. The next objection is again on page 3. That is the seventh paragraph on page 3, which is paragraph 18, which begins --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. The next objection is on page 3, and it is paragraph 18 on page 3, which begins, "It is of note..." Now, that sentence reads: "It is of note that the elementary school visited by Radovan Karadzic was later used as a detention facility for Muslims that lived in the following areas," and it lists some --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that you would like to know why the witness thinks this is of note?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. If it's merely a question of somebody visiting a school at some earlier point, it's hardly of any evidential value whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I can ask him the basis for his conclusion, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's do that then. So that's about -- that the basis of the knowledge of the witness for the observations he makes in paragraph 18. Your next objection, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. Just in relation to the last sentence in that same paragraph, "It had also transpired that the other visitor, Rajko Kusic, had overall command over this detention facility when it was used as such." Again, it's a bold statement without any supporting basis in terms of basis of knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, any problem in --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Same response, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So this will specifically be dealt with in the examination of the witness. Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Now, in page 4 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, if you put on your headphones then you immediately note that you're not using your microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honours. Now, if we go to page 4, the seventh paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that it's 25 and starting with, "It was obvious..."

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you wonder why it was obvious.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, same answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Same answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Again, Your Honours, this just is an indication of how sloppy these statements are. Now, if we move on, then, to paragraph 26. Again, it's the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You wonder why he was aware of Kusic. Is that -- he says, "I'm aware."

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Same answer, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Same answer, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Proceed, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And then we go to paragraph 29. Again, personal view. "My personal view is that this was an early test to see how the Muslims would react." Again, on the basis of opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I intend to ask him specifically about that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll then hear his evidence on that specific part of -- what we find in the statement. Ms. Loukas, next.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Now we go to page 7, and that is the very last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: "My experiences during this time have convinced me that everything the Serbs have carried out --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that you wonder why these experiences were that he could base his conviction upon.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. I mean, as an expression of opinion, it is wholly objectable -- objectionable on the basis on which it is expressed there in the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Same response, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. We'll then hear the evidence of what the experience was, and the Chamber will then see whether it could adopt any conclusions similar as the witness seems to have drawn.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. I would ask that that particular paragraph actually be excised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, let's first hear the evidence. As you know, certainly there's this matter which should be dealt with in examination-in-chief, and I do understand that Mr. Harmon is going to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, I understand that, Your Honour. Now, just going to the second last paragraph on the same page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Again, another indication of how sloppily put together these statements are. That paragraph speaks about various matters in a generalised form without indicating a basis for knowledge, whether it be hearsay, whether it be firsthand hearsay, whether it be secondhand hearsay, what have you. And again I'm sure Mr. Harmon will give the same answer, which is that, you know, these matters will be elicited in evidence in chief, but as a basis for using statements under 89(F) without proper evidence in chief, I do make my generalised objection to using statements that aren't formulated in a proper manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If I look at your observations, Ms. Loukas, it seems that you say you do not know what the basis is. You mention a few possibilities, not one of them being direct observation by the witness himself, which of course if that would be the case, then --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: It should be stated in the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if I say the car came to my house, of course you'd say -- then you should say, "I saw the car coming to my house," or "I heard from some other people that the car came to my house." It should be clear. I take it that, Mr. Harmon, that the examination-in-chief could give further explanation of this part.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It can, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll then expect, before we decide on the admission, then first hear the evidence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I would make one further point and that is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: -- it's all very well that these matters will be explored in evidence chief but it's a shame the Defence hears about the exploration for the first time in evidence in chief and nevertheless the statements are put in under 89(F), because one might say, well, we're dealing with the crime base, but, Your Honour, this is significant in terms of ensuring that evidence is taken in a proper form so that linkages, potential linkages can be looked at in a proper form as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Loukas, if we would have a traditional viva voce testimony, would it be any different? You would have the statement, you would for the first time hear any further or even perhaps the witness might have answered questions only in cross-examination. Isn't that the usual course?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: The usual course is to ensure that statements are taken properly in the first place, Your Honour, and not full of generalised statements of the nature -- and objectionable material, as do the nature of these statements. Particularly when we're dealing with gradations of knowledge in terms of firsthand knowledge, firsthand hearsay, secondhand hearsay. When that sort of aspect is not delineated. And when one looks, for example, at the Bosnian statement, that -- the basis of knowledge at various points in that statement is not delineated, and at various points what time the witness is talking about is not delineated. Neither of the statements are particularly impressive in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand that you would rather -- of course, the Bosnian statement is taken beyond the responsibility of the --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Oh, indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But in general terms I would agree that the lesser questions are open after reading this statement, the better it would be if Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. we used the 89(f) and 92 bis procedures.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I've dealt with my objections in relation to this material. The only other point I would make, and this is in terms of making the Trial Chamber aware of how we'll be proceeding this week, I will be dealing with all four witnesses this week, and I can indicate in relation to that, Your Honours, that in terms of dealing with the balancing of the priorities within a very small Defence team, Your Honours will be aware that Mr. Stewart dealt with the three witnesses last week. I'm dealing with the four witness this week. While Mr. Stewart was dealing with the three witnesses last week, I was dealing with other matters relating to the case in terms of experts. The witness folders were not given to me until Wednesday evening of last week because that's been part of the ruthless organising of priorities that has to be undertaken by the Defence team, and of course Your Honours have indicated in relation to both the applications that we've made for further time for preparation that Your Honours would keep an eye on the situation in relation to Defence preparation, and I think Your Honours should be aware of how much time we've had to curtail the time we spend on witness preparation in order to ensure that we're also spending some time on balancing other priorities in terms of Defence preparation, and I -- I place that on the record, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course to the extent possible the Chamber tries to take into consideration your concerns. At the same time, I see that these witnesses, at least some of them, the 92 bis witnesses, I remember having studied them already thoroughly in -- last November, I think, when we had to decide on the admission and cross-examination but --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Of course they have to be reviewed since last November, of course, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I make that point because I think it is important and the Trial Chamber has indicated that it is interested to see what's occurring because ultimately it does affect the fairness of the trial, and of course the Trial Chamber is interested in that and has expressed an interest in being informed as to the progress of the Defence preparation and the balancing of our priorities. And of course the Defence do not have the luxury of having a different lawyer for each witness this week, and I make that point, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the Chamber has to decide on paragraphs 6 to 10 as to the objection about relevance. This evidence can be led. It has some relevance and context can be created, if necessary, by the Defence. Madam Usher, would you please escort Mr. Alajbegovic into the courtroom. Ms. Loukas, I take it your objections have no consequences as such for the 89(f) summary because that's rather general and is not affected by your objections, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. In terms of the way that Your Honours dealt with the objections this morning, I think that, yes, there's no question in relation to the actual summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Alajbegovic. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Alajbegovic, before you give evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but truth. The text will be handed out to you now by Madam Usher, and I'd like to invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Alajbegovic. Please be seated. You'll first be examined by Mr. Harmon, counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Harmon, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. And if I could have the usher's assistance in moving the ELMO a little farther toward the interpretation booth. We will be using the ELMO in the course of this examination. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Harmon:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Alajbegovic, could you please state your name and spell your last name for the record.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Ramiz Alajbegovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you spell your last name for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. A-l-a-j-b-e-g-o-v-i-c diacritic. R-a-m-i-z.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Alajbegovic. I'm now going to take you through some specifics as to your background. I'm going to read certain items and then I'm going to ask you to affirm the correctness of those items. So let me begin. Mr. Alajbegovic, you are a Bosniak. You were born on the 16th of May, 1954, in the village of Kopljevic in the municipality of Rogatica. You attended elementary school in Rogatica, and you attended secondary school in Sarajevo. Later, you attended Higher School of Internal Affairs in Belgrade and received a degree as a lawyer for internal affairs. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, from 1975 until the present time, you have been engaged in police work and you have held a variety of positions. I'm going to list those positions - not all positions but most of those positions - and I'm going to ask you to affirm what I have stated. In 1975 to 1979, you were a police officer in the former Federal Secretariat for Internal Affairs in Belgrade. From 1979 to 1991 you were a police officer in Rogatica where you held various posts culminating with holding the position as head of the Uniform Police for the public security station in Rogatica. After you fled from Rogatica, you held various positions in the public security station in Gorazde. And from October of 1993 to 1995, you were the deputy commander and then the commander of the Special Police in Gorazde. From 1995 to 1997, you were the deputy commander and then the commander of the police in the Ilijas municipality, a period of 19 months. From mid-1997 to mid-1999, you were the commander of the police in Novi Grad. From mid-1999 to 2001, you were the commander of the police station in Ilidza. From April of 2001 to 2003, in Novi Grad, you were an independent criminal investigator, and from 2003 to the present, you were the chief of the operative centre first police administration in Sarajevo. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to present you with two exhibits. If we could have those exhibits distributed. They are, first of all, a statement that you made, Mr. Alajbegovic, to an investigating judge of the High Court in Sarajevo in criminal proceedings that were pending against an individual named Mico Andric, and the second document is a statement that you provided to the Office of the Prosecutor investigators. Those will be handed up to you in just a moment, and you'll have them placed in front of you. If I could have the exhibit numbers starting with the Bosnian statement.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Prosecution Exhibit P565. And the ICTY statement dated 26 January, 1999, will be Prosecution Exhibit P566.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Alajbegovic, if you could take Prosecution Exhibit 565, which is the statement that was made to an investigating judge in Sarajevo. Do you have that in front of you?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And have you had an opportunity to review that statement before coming into court?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you pointed out two corrections you would like me to make in this statement, and I will direct the Court first of all to paragraph 1 of the statement. And I direct you, Mr. Alajbegovic, as well to the paragraph that's marked number 1, the second sentence in paragraph 1. The date 1974 should be changed to 1979. Is that correct, Mr. Alajbegovic?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The second correction you pointed out to me is on -- is in paragraph 10 of the statement. On the English version, Your Honour, it's on page 7. And third line from the bottom of what's paragraph 10, the number 14 should be corrected to reflect the number 15. So the sentence would read: "The letter also said that we should hand in all our weapons to Mico Andric in Kosovo and that we had to send our answer no later than 1200 hours on 15 August..." and it goes on. Now, with those two corrections made in this statement that you made to the investigating judge, is this an accurate statement and do you adopt this statement for these proceedings?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if we can turn to the statement that you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor investigators on the 26th of January, 1999. If we could turn to that statement. Mr. Alajbegovic, have you had an opportunity to review this statement that you gave to Office of the Prosecutor investigators in your language?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you pointed out to me a number of corrections that needed to be made in this statement, and I'm going to direct you and direct the Court to those corrections.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we start, Your Honours, at paragraph 6. The words after the first word "In" in paragraph 6, the words "April and May" should be inserted. The next correction, Your Honour, is in paragraph 7. At the end the first sentence in the English version, if we strike the word "in" and insert in its place the words "between approximately 2 and 5 August." And the then the second correction is "1990" should be changed to "1991." The next correction appears in paragraph 11 on page 3 of the English. The first name, Milorad Planojevic, Milorad should be stricken and the name should be Dusan, D-u-s-a-n. In that same list of names, the last name has an aka, Zvjerka. That aka should belong to the name above it. So Milorad Mijatovic is the person who was also known as Zvjerka. The next correction, Your Honour, is on -- in paragraph 20. The next correction, Your Honours, is in paragraph 20. The words "February or" in the first sentence should be stricken. So the sentence should read: "The second visit was in March of 1992 ..." Next I refer Your Honours to paragraph 22, the first line. The words "The following day" should be stricken, and in its place the words "In the days that followed..." That very same change should be made in paragraph 23, striking the first two words "That day," and inserting in its place "In the days that followed..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now it becomes a bit unclear to me, Mr. Harmon, because if we change in 22, "From this meeting in the days that followed," and if you start 23 again with, "In the days that followed," that could be after the days that followed the set up of roadblocks or the days or it could be the days that followed the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me clarify that on the examination, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The next correction, Your Honour, is a misspelling that appears in paragraph 26. The name of the village "Pesuzici" should be properly spelled. The correct spelling is P-e-r-s-u-r-i-c-i, and there is a banana over the S and a half banana over the C. The next correction is in paragraph 34. The words "I was" following "In my opinion" should be stricken, and the words "they were" inserted in its place. So the sentence would read, "In my opinion, they were being told..." Paragraph 37, the second and third words in the first sentence, "remember seeing" should be stricken and in its place "received information about" should be inserted. The next correction is in a spelling in paragraph 41. It appears in the English version on the bottom of page 5. The village "Kukavica," if you strike the last letter A and insert the letter E, it will be properly spelled. Paragraph 42, you strike the first word -- strike the first "Later, at 1145 exactly..." If you strike those words and in its place insert the words "On 22 May 1992 at 1200 hours..." And the last correction is in paragraph 43. The word "aircraft" that appears in the third line of the English should be preceded by the word "anti" and followed by the word "weapons." So it should be "subjected to an attack from tanks, artillery, and anti-aircraft weapons." Now, those are the corrections that Mr. Alajbegovic pointed out to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Alajbegovic, with those corrections having been made, do you adopt this statement for purposes of these proceedings today?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could read then a summary of the written evidence that will be tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just for practical reasons, I take it you will provide a corrected version then finally if it would be admitted. Is there any need to copy it all again? I made all the changes. I could live with this copy for my personal file.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I've made corrections on my copy as we've gone along as well, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So one copy would do for the registrar so we know that's the final version presented.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So there is no need, Mr. Harmon, to cut another wood for --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me then read a summary for the public of what is contained in this written evidence. "The OTP is submitting the written evidence of Ramiz Alajbegovic. This written evidence consists of a statement that he provided to the Office of the Prosecutor and statement that he provided to an investigating judge of the High Court in Sarajevo. "Mr. Alajbegovic is a Bosniak from the municipality of Rogatica where, prior to the war, he was the chief of the Uniform Police. "In his written evidence, Mr. Alajbegovic describes Rogatica as a multi-ethnic community living in harmony. "He was present at Serb rallies in 1991 that were overtly nationalistic in tone, where various Serb speakers spoke of Serb nationalism and the desire to build a Greater Serbia. "Mr. Alajbegovic identifies the main SDS leaders of Rogatica and he discusses their activities in encouraging Serb nationalism. "He also describes two occasions when Radovan Karadzic came to Rogatica municipality and met with local SDS officials, including Rajko Kusic. "He describes the increase of tensions between the Muslim and Serb communities caused by, among other things, the presence and conduct of paramilitary formations from Serbia, the White Eagles, and local paramilitary formations under the command of Rajko Kusic. "Mr. Alajbegovic's written evidence describes meetings with SDS representatives. At one such meeting, he was informed by Rajko Kusic that 'there was no future for Muslims in this area and that the Muslims would be attacked' if they did not leave. "His written evidence describes the arming of Serbs in the Rogatica municipality by the JNA and the disarming of Muslim villages. "In respect of the disarming of Muslim villages, he describes a series of ultimatums from Rajko Kusic that were directed to the inhabitants of those villages to hand over their weapons in exchange for which they were promised they could continue to live in the municipality. His evidence shows that these were false promises. "His written evidence identifies the commencement of the war in Rogatica on the 22nd of May, 1992, shortly after the arrival of the Uzice Corps. He describes attacks on various Muslim villages and the consequences of those attacks, specifically the killing of people and the razing of villages."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Alajbegovic, your evidence is going to be dealing with the Rogatica municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, if I could first direct your attention to Prosecution Exhibit 527. I'd like to direct your attention to three pages in this exhibit, and the first page, Your Honour, is page 3. If page 3 could be shown to the witness as well. Your Honour, on page 3 I'd like to direct your attention to two features of this. Rogatica is located on the east, next to Visegrad and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. next to Sarajevo. You will see in -- Your Honours, that it is in part territory that is contiguous with Sarajevo. If Your Honours turn to page 25, Your Honours will see that that part of Rogatica is contiguous with Pale canton, which is part of Sarajevo. And finally, Your Honours, on page 23 itself is the map of the Rogatica municipality identifying a number of the villages and the main roads.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Alajbegovic, I pointed out that the municipality of Rogatica is next to Pale. Can you tell the Court approximately -- the approximate distance between the city of Rogatica and the city of Pale?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC
utterances.text: About 65 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court the approximate distance between the city of Rogatica and the location in the Han Pijesak municipality where the army of the Republika Srpska had its main headquarters?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC
utterances.text: About 65 to 70 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now -- I'm finished with that large map. Thank you, Madam Usher. If we could turn to the next exhibit. This next exhibit, Your Honours, is a demographic -- a map of Rogatica municipality. It shows the demographic distribution of people. And you will notice, Your Honours, that the statistics above the map, in the left-hand corner, these statistics are based on the 1991 census.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Alajbegovic, you have before you a copy of the next exhibit, which is --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit P567.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- 567. You had an opportunity before coming to court to look at this map, have you not, Mr. Alajbegovic?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this exhibit shows that the majority population in the Rogatica municipality, the majority ethnic group was the Muslims; correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does this map accurately show the villages that were majority Muslim and majority Serb?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in respect of --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm finished with that map. If that could be kept on the ELMO. We're going to be referring to it throughout the testimony.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Alajbegovic, can you -- strike that. Was there a significant and main road that went -- that traversed the Rogatica municipality from Serbia to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during the course of the war in Croatia and the course of the war in Slovenia, was that route used for convoys of military equipment?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that road that went through Rogatica municipality strategically significant, in your view?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Very strategic it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why do you say that?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Because the forces of the Yugoslav People's Army used it to transport its units and military formations, weapons and equipment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, before the war started, Mr. Alajbegovic, can you describe what life was like in the Rogatica municipality. And when I say what life was like, what the relations were between the Muslim community and the Serb community in that municipality.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Very good, solid, and good-neighbourly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did the relations -- just approximately, when did those relations start to change?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC
utterances.text: At the point when the war broke out in Croatia and when the Muslim -- the Muslim recruits for the Territorial Defence refused to go to the Croatian battleground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll get into that in a little greater detail a little bit later, but let me now, Mr. Alajbegovic, refer you to your statement. That is the statement 566, the statement you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor. If you could please turn to paragraph 11 of that statement. You're going to be referring in the course of your testimony this morning to certain names, and we're going to be hearing about them, and I would like you to assist the Trial Chamber in identifying these people, who they were and what bodies they belonged to. Specifically, if we could start with Rajko Kusic. First of all, did you know Rajko Kusic personally?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I knew him personally, Rajko Kusic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you meet with him prior to the war and meetings where you were a negotiator on behalf of the Muslim --

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- community?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you identify what organisations Rajko Kusic belonged to?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Rajko Kusic belonged to the SDS membership, the Main Board of the SDS, in fact, for Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Serbian Democratic Party, that is. He was a member of the SDS board for Rogatica, and he was also the commander of the Serb army in Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'd like to, while we're on Mr. Kusic, introduce the next two exhibits, Your Honour, and have those distributed. One is an excerpt, Your Honour, from Prosecution Exhibit 37, and rather than introduce the whole exhibit I've, for your convenience, excerpted the relevant parts of Prosecution Exhibit 37. If Your Honours turn on -- Exhibit 37 was stenographic notes of a meeting of the SDS party that was held on the 12th of July 1991, and if Your Honours turn to the first page, which is 94 in this excerpt, you will see the 45 members who have been elected to the Main Board. The first name that appears is Momcilo Krajisnik. And if you turn the page, you will see item number 39, Rajko Kusic, as being a member of the Main Board. If I could distribute the next exhibit as well. This exhibit, Your Honours -- this exhibit is -- could we have the number, Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Alajbegovic, you've seen this document before coming into court; correct? And this is a document --

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this is a document, we see, from the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, Rogatica brigade commander. It's dated the 1st of August, 1992, and at the end of the document it bears the signature of an individual below the typed words "Commander, Rogatica brigade." The name is Rajko Kusic. Does this confirm what you have testified to, that Mr. Kusic was the commander of the Rogatica brigade?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's not a proper question. I mean, that's ultimately a matter for the Trial Chamber. To ask a witness, in relation to a document that he hasn't seen before other than the Prosecution showing him the document, is simply not an appropriate way of eliciting evidence. And evidence is not placing a document in front of a witness and saying, "Does this confirm..." That is a matter for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I will rephrase the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this document showing that Rajko Kusic is the commander of the Rogatica Brigade consistent with the information that you knew in 1992?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Most certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we could then turn to the next name on this paragraph 11 of your OTP statement. Sveto Veselinovic. Could you tell the Court about Mr. Veselinovic. What political party did he belong to?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Sveto Veselinovic belonged to the Serbian Democratic Party, and he was its president for Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we could turn to the next name on the paragraph 11; Mladen Vasiljevic. Can you tell the Chamber what political party he belonged to?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Mladen Vasiljevic belonged to the Serbian Democratic Party in Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What position did he ultimately hold in Rogatica?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC
utterances.text: He was appointed commander of the public security station in Rogatica. And then he became head of the Serbian police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And before the war started, was he a colleague of yours in the police?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next name, if we could turn to the name of Dusan Planojevic, can you tell the Court what political party he belonged to?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Dusan Planojevic belonged to the Serbian Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally Mile Ujic. Can you tell us about Mile Ujic, what political party he belonged to.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Mile Ujic was a member of the Serbian Democratic Party in Rogatica, and he discharged the functions of the Prime Minister of the municipal government of Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honours will be hearing about these names in the course of the examination.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in paragraphs 6 and 7 of your ICTY statement, you describe two rallies, and I'd like to focus, first of all, your attention on paragraph 6, the rally that occurred in April or May of 1991. Were you present at that rally, Mr. Alajbegovic?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why were you present?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC
utterances.text: We, the public security station, were responsible for ensuring that the rally in front of the church went through peacefully, we as the police force.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did that rally occur in the city of Rogatica itself?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in front of the church on the plateau.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you -- were you present throughout the complete duration of the rally?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC
utterances.text: No, not throughout, but we came from time to time and inspected.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during that rally, did you have an opportunity to hear certain speakers addressing the crowd?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How large was the crowd?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC
utterances.text: There were over 3.000 people present.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were those -- were you able to identify what ethnic group those people were who were attending the rally?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC
utterances.text: There were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you identify in paragraph 6 -- you said, "Also speaking at this ceremony were a number of Serb nationalists," and you identify somebody you believe to be a writer named Krsmanovic. Did you hear Mr. Krsmanovic speak?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I heard parts of the speech because I couldn't stay there all the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you relate to the Judges what parts of Mr. Krsmanovic's speech you heard.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krsmanovic said in his speech, among other things, that people should rally around the cause of Serbian unity, and he was inciting hatred between Muslims and Serbs. He said that Serbs would not allow Bosnia to secede and the genocide of 1945 to be repeated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any local SDS --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: '41, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any local SDS political figures address the crowd?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which SDS political figures from Rogatica addressed the crowd?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC
utterances.text: The first to address the crowd was Sveto Veselinovic, president of the SDS, and the last speaker was Rajko Kusic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the content of their speeches to the crowd?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Both of them echoed the speech of Mr. Krsmanovic, and throughout their speeches they were applauded by the crowd. Both of them said the time had come for the Serbian people to unite and to create an integral state. They said they would not allow Bosnia to secede from Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, at this particular rally, can you describe the -- what else was taking place besides speeches?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Mass popular celebrations followed. People danced the kola dance, waved Serbian flags, sang Chetnik songs "From the Topola tree to the fields," and the famous song, "Who says that Serbia's small? It isn't small. It waged a war three times." Those songs were sung the whole day during that rally, that popular gathering.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did this -- did this rally have any effect on the attitudes of people within the municipality and the ethnic harmony that you described earlier?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the effect of this rally and these speeches?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC
utterances.text: The insecurity of the Bosniak people. They were certain that they heard the message correctly, that there would be no peaceful co-existence in that territory and that the worst was a distinct possibility, namely deportation or ethnic cleansing, and that proved to be correct later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if I could direct your attention, Mr. Alajbegovic, to a second rally that's described in paragraph 7 of your statement. This is the rally that took place in the village of Borike between approximately the 2nd and the 5th of August, 1991. Did you attend that rally?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did attend together with the police forces intended to secure the rally, because the organiser of the gathering was the SDS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And approximately how many people were present during that rally?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC
utterances.text: There were over 5.000 people present, all of them Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you hear any speeches at that particular rally?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I did. The same speakers addressed the people at this rally as well; Krsmanovic, Kusic, and Veselinovic, plus some others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you inform the Trial Chamber the contents of the speeches of Mr. Veselinovic and Mr. Kusic?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC
utterances.text: The speech of Mr. Rajko Kusic was almost the same as his speech before the church in April, May. It was met with constant applause. And Sveto Veselinovic also repeated his speech from before the church, only this time he went even further by saying that the Drina River had never really been the border, it was only the gap between two lungs. That is what impressed me and the other police officers, Bosniak police officers, who provided security at that meeting. We had a feeling that this was an introduction into the integration of Serbian lands. This speech was later printed in the newspapers the next day and the days that followed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did a representative of the SDA party speak at this particular rally?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was that and what was the nature of his speech?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC
utterances.text: It was Mr. Asim Pavica. He spoke before Rajko Kusic and Sveto Veselinovic. He spoke about the need to live together, to be tolerant, and to preserve peace in that area. It was a very brief speech.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall how that speech was received?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Some of those present applauded, but others gave him the raspberry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let me direct your attention to a paragraph in your statement. It's paragraph 12 in your statement. If would you read that paragraph to yourself. I want to direct your attention specifically to the last sentence in that paragraph. Have you read that paragraph to yourself?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The last sentence reads: "In my opinion, there was no threat to them whatsoever, and this was mainly an attempt to brainwash them and to encourage Serb nationalism." Can you --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Just in relation to that, Your Honour, that was the portion of the sentence that was actually excised from the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just re-read. It's my recollection, Mr. Harmon, that I asked you to elicit this evidence from the witness in examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But there might have been some doubt in respect of the other elements, because we started excising that and then later on we have several times found a solution that a proper foundation, factual foundation, would be laid. So I can imagine that perhaps the distinction between the paragraph 12 and the others might not have been. But as a matter of fact, Mr. Harmon, you were invited to elicit from the witness the factual basis perhaps before asking him to read what the result of it all is.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for the sake of clarity of the record, at the bottom of page 5 and the top of page 6 of today's transcript in the LiveNote is where the excision is dealt with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'll have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If there is an excision, I'm happy to excise it, Your Honour. I obviously made an error when I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you could perhaps put questions to the witness in relation to it without directly relating to the -- to the text as we see it on paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then in this paragraph, sir, you identify certain people who are named in that paragraph as travelling around Serb villages, telling them Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that there was a Muslim threat and that they had to protect themselves. Sir, can you first of all identify the time period when these people were travelling around to the Serb villages?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC
utterances.text: The period -- it was the period of 1992, January, February.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in your opinion, was what these people were informing the local Serb residents of those villages correct?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC
utterances.text: That was not correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why do you say that?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Because there was no danger whatsoever that the Muslim people would attack Serbs, because we, on the contrary, were in favour of peaceful co-existence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have a view as to why Mr. Bojovic and Mr. Planojevic and Milorad Sokolovic were going to these Serb villages to inform the residents that there was a danger?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just in relation to that, "Do you have a view," the view expressed is a matter to which I've objected to and the matter that has been excised. If Mr. Harmon wants to elicit factual matters that may assist the Trial Chamber, that's one thing, but to get the witness just to express the view is not the appropriate way of dealing with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Alajbegovic, try to forget the formulation as it was put to you by Mr. Harmon. Did you form an opinion on the reasons why Mr. Bojovic and Mr. Planojevic and Milorad Sokolovic went to the Serb villages, telling the people about the danger? And could you tell us, if you have formed such an opinion, on the basis of what you formed that opinion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did. At that moment, members of the government were aware that these activists were down on the ground, and that was later confirmed by Serbs, by Serb representatives, because not even they were prepared to take up arms against their neighbours at that moment. However, after Sokolovic, Bojovic, and Dusan arrived as persons of authority, the latter were brainwashed. They embraced the ideas of the SDS, and they put themselves at the disposal of the Serbian Democratic Party in the aims of creating the Serbian municipality of Rogatica and thereby Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One additional -- perhaps two additional questions. The first one: How did you know that the government was aware of, as you said, these activists were down on the ground? And if you're talking about the government, perhaps you also explain what government exactly you had in mind.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I meant then and I still mean the legally elected authorities in Rogatica. They consisted -- that government consisted of the SDA, the SDS, and smaller opposition parties, because we had in that area our people in the police force. At that moment, we still had joint police patrols, and that kind of information would reach me as chief of the Uniformed Police. I passed it on to the president of the municipality, and chief the public security station, who was also president of the SDA. They made certain conclusions which proved to be right in later practice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I would have first one additional question. You told us that the local Serbs were not inclined, at least not before the -- these visits, to take up arms against their neighbours. How did you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One part. We're only talking about one part of the territory. For instance, the local commune of Kozici, where I lived and where I went to work every day. So I was able to receive information from some Serbs and from police officers who came to these conclusions, because later arms supply began together with actual use of arms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. One point of clarification. So about these two meetings you mentioned, these two rallies in April, May, and August 1991. I just would like to know whether in that region it was common for such meetings to take place, for such meetings to take place along community lines. Was it usual before April for a community to have such meetings for -- when there was some religious occasion or other?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not in this form, but it was normal to mark national holidays with some limits to decent behaviour, and Serbs and Muslims would even march together because it was a common land.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These meetings, how was your own presence perceived by people, whether -- how did they react?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand the question. Do you mean these rallies or the previous ones?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I'm talking about these two meetings, the meetings you mentioned in your statement. You were there to provide security, to supervise the meeting. Was there any reaction you noticed because of your presence there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Harmon. And we'd like to have a break within the next three to five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very briefly, Mr. Alajbegovic, I would like to direct your attention to the situation of arming of the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And Your Honours, for your information, that's found in paragraph 4 of the Bosnian statement and paragraphs 15, 16, 37 and 38 of the statements given to the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we get to those particular paragraphs, can you tell the Court, Mr. Alajbegovic, what happened to the weapons that were stored in the Territorial Defence warehouse in Rogatica?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I can tell you. The weapons that were in the premises on the Territorial Defence headquarters in Rogatica were located in 1990 to the barracks in Han Pijesak, and it was placed under the control of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did that occur?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the effect of the removal of the Territorial Defence, the weapons from the Territorial Defence warehouse in terms of the availability of arms to people who were in the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC
utterances.text: It was placed under the control of the Yugoslav People's Army, and it was no longer accessible to either ethnic community.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this point, if you would like, I'm prepared to stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a break for 25 minutes. We will restart at five minutes to eleven. Not by the clock of this courtroom, because by the clock of this courtroom it will be five minutes to ten.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Alajbegovic, we are on the topic now of the arming of the Serbs, and I want to direct your attention to paragraphs 37 and 38 of your statement. This describes receiving information about the arming of the population in the area of Stavanj. Can you please tell us approximately when the incident that is referred to in paragraphs 37 and 38 occurred.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was the period of October 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you could take a look at the exhibit -- Prosecution Exhibit 567 that is on the ELMO, and if you could use a pointer, could you just indicate with the pointer the area where this particular incident occurred.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Stavanj, Stara Borike, Agarovici, and Stara Gora.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And for the record, that is on the eastern side of Prosecution Exhibit 567. Thank you very much. Now, briefly can you explain what information you received, from whom you received that information, and what you did as a result of receiving that information.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We - that is I and the chief of the public security station of Rogatica - received information on the premises of the police station from someone we knew, a local of the village of Medna Luka, to the effect that three days before, in a place called Stavanj, weapons were handed out by the Yugoslav People's Army, with two military trucks taking part, and there was an official police vehicle there belonging to the Rogatica public security station, and Mladen Vasiljevic, the then commander, was also there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Based on that information, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC
utterances.text: We consulted each other, and the next day I, as the head of the public security station, and the crime inspector who worked with us at the time, together with Mladen Vasiljevic got into an official vehicle, and we suggested that we go and check out the area of the local community of Borike, and he agreed to do that. While we were driving towards Borike - I did the driving myself - I suggested that we tour the area around the Stavanj location and take the dirt road to the Borike locality. He agreed to that but I could feel that he was nervous. When we reached the Stavanj area where there was a traffic sign, I said that we would carry on for another 1 to 200 metres and then turn left into the woods there because the unidentified person had given us information to the effect that it was in that area where we would find the remainders of the original cartons and packaging of the weapons belonging to the Yugoslav People's Army, the crates, and they had contained automatic rifles, M53 machine-guns, and M84 machine-guns. We got out of the car, and according to what the man had said, we took to the left into the woods. We found two locations, and we found the remnants of the cartons from which the weapons had been distributed. And nearby the Serbs or, rather, the inhabitants of the villages had been issued the weapons the previous day where Mladen Vasiljevic was present. And they roasted some lambs there, and they celebrated that day, probably for having completed their operation successfully. We managed to take photographs and document the situation we came across, so we have a set of photographs illustrating that whole event and what we came upon. And Mladen told me at that point in time, he said, "Ramiz, yes, it's true, I was there, but please don't tell anybody, any of the SDS representatives, because it could cost me my life." He said, "The worst could happen to me." After that, we left that area and went to the hotel at Borike, had a cup of coffee together, and then returned to the public security station of Rogatica. We compiled a photographic album with all the documentations and compiled proposals for the republican SUP of BH, Bosnia-Herzegovina. And I personally the very next day handed a copy of that set of documents to the SUP, the crime department there of the SUP where Momcilo Mandic was the chief. And since we knew that the information and data were not something that he could deal with because he would dilute it, we took it to his first assistant, the head of a department of the crime police, and that man's name was Hasib Dazdarevic. And after that we received no feedback information as to what we should do, what steps we should take in cases of that kind, although Mr. Dazdarevic did suggest at the time that what we proposed wouldn't mean a great deal. That is to say we wanted to conduct a search. He said that this would only complicate matters and that's where the whole thing stopped.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In respect of the cartons that you described, and you've described the types of weapon boxes, were these boxes JNA boxes? Did they have JNA written on --

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to conclude, based on the number of boxes you saw, the volume of weapons that had been distributed in the area on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you inform the Trial Chamber what the volume of weapons that had been -- weapons and ammunition that had been distributed?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were over 50 pieces of long-barrelled automatic weapons and over 50.000 bullets of different calibres for the weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, I would like to direct your attention to paragraphs 15 and 16 of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, would you -- I apologise. I have one additional question. Could you tell us, Mr. Alajbegovic, whether Mr. Vasiljevic explained why he feared for his life if you would report to the SDS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes. He was quite clear in what he said and meant. If the SDS were to learn about that, it would have meant that he had disclosed the operation conducted by the JNA, which was in cohorts with the SDS from Rogatica and probably the Main Staff of the SDS of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So he feared for being negligent in hiding the operation. Is that a correct understanding? Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for the record, if the witness would answer audibly it would be a clearer record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I had forgotten. If you just nod, it does not appear in the transcript. So I saw your nodding vertically, which means confirmation of what I said; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Alajbegovic, if we could turn to paragraphs 15 and 16 of your statement where you describe being an eyewitness to the distribution of arms. Could you, first of all, give us an approximate date or time when that distribution took place in your presence.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. All this took place at the beginning of 1991 in the close vicinity of the church, or more exactly by the house next to the church in the Donje Polje settlement in the town of Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court precisely what you saw.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Towards evening, the employees of the police who were located on the main road running from Sarajevo to Rogatica, the place called Stjenice, which is where a reserve police station existed, informed through the communication lines, informed me, they used my code number, and said that there was an official vehicle, police vehicle, driven by Mr. Mladen Vasiljevic, the commander at the time, that it was driving along, and behind him was a truck who was being -- which was being driven by Limic, who was known as Garo, and that there was a military truck behind his car, and it was assumed that they were driving in weapons from the barracks at Han Pijesak. At the time, we followed the vehicle. The policemen on duty in the field followed the vehicle from the entrance to town until it turned a corner across the church and the church house, where all these vehicles stopped with Mr. Mladen and the man called Limic and two members of the Yugoslav People's Army. And at that point from the direction of Donje Polje, which is inhabited by Serbs, another vehicle arrived, a TAM truck, and two to three tractors, or two large tractors and one smaller tractor, and after that, they started unloading the crates of -- or boxes of ammunition and hand-held rocket launchers from those vehicles. I saw Mladen myself there. He was standing there, providing security, and in front of him up to the main road there was a member of the reserve force, police force, and his name was Zeljko Rajak. He had been in the police force until quite recently. I don't know why he's not working there any more. And then there were activists coming in from the local commune of Kozici, and they took over the weapons, loaded them up into their own vehicles and transported them to the villages and the Kozici local commune, which area was inhabited by the Serbs. They reached the Mokri Lug area and took them to the house of Milenko Obradovic, and that's where the distribution point was to distribute the weapons to the different villages and issue them out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me then ask you some additional questions. Did you see a JNA vehicle at the location where these arms were distributed?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I said that and I confirm it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you see, the person who was driving that JNA vehicle, how was he dressed?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC
utterances.text: They were dressed in army uniforms, the JNA army uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you say that a certain activist came to that location. Can you identify by name the activists who came and what party they were associated with?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Dr. Radan Bojovic was there, and then there was Milos Rajak with his TAM truck. Then there was Mico Andric, and a certain man by the name of Rajko Ikonic. He was also an activist from the local commune area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So were the people you've just identified associated with any particular political party, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were all members of the Serbian Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, can you take a look at the exhibit that's to your right, Prosecution Exhibit 567, the map of the Rogatica municipality, and with a pointer can you indicate the area that you say is Kozici and where those arms were then taken.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There's a local road which isn't indicated on the map, Jevcici. Drobnici, Starcici. Starcici is here. Trnovo. Starcici, Trnovo, Pljevcici, and then there as the little hamlet of Kosovo which isn't on the map between Pljevcici and Kozici. Bunjevac, not on the map. It's also a small place, a hamlet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said that Mladen Vasiljevic was also present at this Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. location and that you saw him there.

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to confront Mr. Vasiljevic about what you had seen; and if you did, what was his reaction?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the next day at the police station, I said, "Mladen, what did all that mean and what's going on?" And he gave me an answer to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his answer?

utterances.speaker: RAMIZ ALAJBEGOVIC
utterances.text: He said, "Well, you see, we have to arm ourselves because you Muslims are arming yourselves too." And I said he wasn't right on that score and that I would inform my superiors along the chain of command. He became nervous at that point, but he wasn't much interested in his police work. He had devoted all his time to the other activities, the party activities, the party to which he belonged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me then direct your attention to another topic, which is visits by Radovan Karadzic to Rogatica, and specifically I'd like to draw your attention to paragraphs 17 to 20 of the statement given to the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes [microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you said, "I told him that I was going to tell my superiors about it." Who were your superiors in fact, and what were you able to do by telling them this? And in fact, did you actually do something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We didn't take any steps, but along the chain of responsibility we were duty-bound, both me and Mladen, to inform our superiors at the SUP and the public security station, the RSUP. He didn't do that, I did, but we couldn't do anything further because they said we would complicate matters, because we knew that the army and the SDS were arming the Serb people and that we couldn't oppose this and stand up to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, but what I fail to understand is there was still a civilian authority there. There was a civilian Ministry of Interior. There was still a hierarchy that was in place. Everything was still functioning. Why did you not then take either your computer or a pen and draft a report and send it directly to the Supreme Commander? You -- you were in the Ministry of Interior, weren't you? That was your superior. Could you please answer this question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We didn't have computers at the time, but we did have a system of communication by telephone. We had telephone links.
